text: The publication strategy is aligned with the progression of the research. The current stage work establishes the conceptual and technical foundation, while the next stage work will strengthen the framework through formal analysis and comprehensive empirical validation.
⦅The research plan is divided into two major stages, the current stage and the next stage.⦆

title: Current Stage: Completed and Current Work

text: The current stage focuses on establishing the foundational trust-oriented authorisation framework. ⦅The main activities are the development of the trust-centric consent model, decentralised identity and authority verification, multi-party authorisation, and policy-aware access control. Temporal and lifecycle enforcement, originally planned for the next stage, has also been implemented in the current stage, as reported in Section 7.5.⦆

The next stage will build upon the foundational trust-oriented ⦅authorisation framework established during the current stage and extend the research towards dynamic consent governance [13, 24], formal security assurance, and comprehensive empirical validation.⦆⦅⦆ ⦅The current stage focuses on establishing the core mechanisms required to construct a trustworthy authorisation decision. The next stage will investigate whether this trust can be maintained over time, formally justified, and reliably demonstrated in practical healthcare data-sharing scenarios.⦆

⦃The next stage activities are planned sequentially. ⦅The formal specification of the security properties will be undertaken first, since the empirical experiments are to be designed against those properties. The performance and adversarial evaluation will follow in the second half of the stage. The lifecycle extensions and integrated evaluation will be completed last, once the formal model is stable.⦆⦄

The ⟪first⟫ focus is formal security assurance. The current stage framework establishes the conceptual relationship between identity verification, collective authorisation, and policy enforcement. ⟪The next⟫ stage will investigate these relationships more rigorously by defining the security properties that the framework is expected to satisfy. The analysis will consider conditions such as invalid identities, insufficient authorisation, policy violations, expired consent, revoked consent, and unauthorised lifecycle transitions. The purpose of this work is not merely to demonstrate that the prototype works under normal conditions, but to establish explicit security properties and determine whether the proposed authorisation model provides the expected protection when relevant security conditions are violated.

The ⟪second⟫ focus is comprehensive empirical validation. The HALAH prototype provides the experimental environment for evaluating the proposed framework using synthetic healthcare data and representative multi-party consent scenarios. ⦅The next stage will extend the current prototype-based evaluation to include both successful and adversarial access requests.⦆ The experiments will examine whether the implementation consistently produces an ALLOW decision only when the required trust conditions are satisfied and produces a DENY decision when one or more required conditions are violated. Particular attention will be given to the relationship between the formal security model and the observed behaviour of the implemented system. The major next stage activities and their expected outcomes are summarised in Table 16.

⦅The performance study will measure the gas cost of the mint and revoke transactions, the block-confirmation latency on Sepolia, the Groth16 proof generation and verification time, and the end-to-end decision latency per access request. In addition, it will report enforcement accuracy as the proportion of adversarial requests that are correctly denied.⦆⦃⦄

⦅The formal component will state two properties. The first is the soundness property Decision(C, R, t) = ALLOW ⇒ V~I~ ∧ V~A~ ∧ V~P~ ∧ V~T~ ∧ V~L~. The second is the lifecycle invariant that no REVOKED or EXPIRED consent can re-enter the ACTIVE state. These properties will be verified by model checking of the state machine or by proof over the predicate definitions of Chapter 6.⦆⦃ The evaluation criterion for this component is that every property is either verified or refuted by an explicit counterexample.⦄

text: ⦅An important analytical objective of the next stage is to examine the relationship between the different forms of trust established throughout the framework.⦆ Temporal validity, for example, should not be treated as an independent access-control feature. Instead, it should act as an additional condition on an already established authorisation relationship. Similarly, revocation should invalidate a previously established consent rather than merely create a new record indicating that the consent has changed. This perspective allows the research to investigate trust as a dynamic property rather than as a one-time outcome of authentication or approval.

⦅The complete authorisation model developed across the current stage and the next stage will therefore be evaluated as a conjunction of independently verifiable conditions.⦆⟪⟫ Conceptually, the final decision can be expressed as
⦅Decision(C, R, t)⦆ = ALLOW

only when the identity and authority of the requester are valid, the required multi-party authorisation has been established, the requested operation satisfies the consent policy, and the consent remains valid according to its temporal and lifecycle state. If any required condition is violated, the framework should produce a denial decision and preserve sufficient evidence to explain the reason for that decision.

From a research perspective, this represents an important transition from static consent management to dynamic trustworthy authorisation. The objective is not to add a collection of independent security mechanisms, but to investigate how these mechanisms jointly contribute to the establishment, maintenance, and verification of trust throughout the consent lifecycle.

⦅By the completion of the next stage, the research is expected to provide three complementary forms of contribution.⦆ First, the research will provide a conceptual Trust Computing model that explains how trustworthy multi-party consent can be established and maintained. Second, it will provide a technical implementation through the HALAH prototype demonstrating how the proposed trust conditions can be enforced in a decentralised healthcare environment. Third, it will provide formal and empirical evidence concerning the security and practical effectiveness of the proposed framework.

⦅Consequently, the next stage will complete the transition from the foundational authorisation mechanisms established in the current stage to a dynamically managed, formally reasoned, and empirically validated⦆⟪⟫ ⟪trust-oriented authorisation framework⟫. ⦅The final contribution will not be assessed simply by whether consent can be recorded or whether access can be granted. It will be assessed by whether the system can provide a defensible basis for determining why an access decision should be trusted. It must also determine when that trust should no longer apply.⦆
